name: MyFitnessPal Premium
tagline: Log user-chosen meals and activity with neutral summaries and no restrictive coaching

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Unlimited-looking manual food and activity logs; 0 barcode scans and 0 Meal Planner recipes
tiers.notes: Ads remain and several macro/analysis tools are paid.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Barcode scanner, custom macros/calorie goals, advanced insights, fasting tools, and no ads
tiers.notes: $79.99 billed annually; app stores still expose lower legacy/alternate $9.99 monthly and $49.99 annual products to some accounts.

tiers.name: Premium+
tiers.limits: Premium features plus Meal Planner with 1,500+ recipes and grocery-list tools
tiers.notes: Monthly and annual billing exist, but the current public official pages did not expose a reliable USD price; 7-day trial advertised.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Free plan: no published cap on manual meal/activity entries; 0 barcode scans and 0 Meal Planner recipes.
pricing.billingTerms: Premium monthly + annual; Premium+ monthly + annual; paid plans auto-renew
pricing.hiddenCosts: Legacy and platform-specific offers can be materially cheaper than the public rate. Premium+ pricing is shown only in some checkout contexts, and HSA/FSA purchase paths can have different trial treatment.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For MyFitnessPal Premium, log user-chosen meals and activity with neutral summaries and no restrictive coaching. The hard boundary is huge food database, barcode data, device integrations, models, and mobile polish, plus hardware data, content, coaching, and trust.
coreLoopDIY: Log user-chosen meals and activity, plan moderate routines, and show neutral summaries and trends without diagnosing, shaming, or enforcing restrictive goals.
requirements: optional HealthKit or Health Connect permission
whatYouLose: huge food database, barcode data, device integrations, models, and mobile polish
large content library and social network
moatNotes: hardware data, content, coaching, and trust
ongoingBurden: sensor permissions, data quality, notifications, safety language, accessibility, sync, privacy, content review, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for MyFitnessPal Premium because people pay for polished mobile capture, trusted content, hardware integration, and coaching rather than the basic logbook. The recurring cost buys sensor permissions, data quality, notifications, safety language, accessibility, sync, privacy, content review, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: wger
priorArt.desc: Active open-source fitness and workout management application.

alternatives.name: OpenNutriTracker
alternatives.desc: Calories, macros and micronutrients stay on your phone; the app declines to become your diet coach.

facts.install: Install the iOS/Android build from the app store or F-Droid
facts.dataFormat: Diary, goals, custom foods, and measurements are stored in encrypted local Hive databases on the phone and can be exported as JSON/CSV; food searches may query the project's Supabase service and Open Food Facts.
facts.gapVsPaid: OpenNutriTracker has a much smaller branded-food and barcode ecosystem and fewer device, restaurant, recipe, and exercise integrations than MyFitnessPal Premium.

alternatives.name: Food You
alternatives.desc: A local Android food diary with proper micronutrients and none of the motivational yelling.

facts.install: Install the Android app from F-Droid or the published APK
facts.dataFormat: The food diary and personal records stay in the app's local database with export/backup options; food searches can contact Open Food Facts, USDA FoodData Central, and the Swiss Food Composition Database.
facts.gapVsPaid: Food You is Android-only and cannot match MyFitnessPal's enormous crowd-sourced food catalog, barcode coverage, restaurant data, integrations, and cross-device social ecosystem.

alternatives.name: Waistline
alternatives.desc: A plain Android calorie diary that keeps its data local and its opinions to itself.

facts.install: Install the Android app from Google Play or F-Droid
facts.dataFormat: Meals, diary entries, foods, goals, and measurements live in a local on-device database with import/export; barcode and food searches can contact Open Food Facts and USDA services.
facts.gapVsPaid: Waistline's local Android diary is simpler and less connected than MyFitnessPal's branded-food database, barcode scanner, recipe importer, device integrations, and cross-platform account.

alternatives.name: wger
alternatives.desc: Meals, workouts and trend charts in one open-source bunker; polish is not the main feature.

facts.install: Create an account on wger.de/use the mobile app, or deploy the official Docker Compose stack
facts.dataFormat: Hosted records live in wger's service; self-hosted users keep accounts, workouts, nutrition, measurements, and exercise data in PostgreSQL plus persistent media volumes, while the mobile client maintains an offline local database and syncs.
facts.gapVsPaid: wger's meal logging is far less comprehensive and convenient than MyFitnessPal's food database, barcode and recipe tools, device integrations, and daily mobile workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: None for the hosted service or mobile app; self-hosting immediately requires Docker Compose, PostgreSQL, Redis/sync services, a reverse proxy, mail, backups, and upgrades.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Premium plan and a personal general-wellbeing tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for MyFitnessPal Premium in an empty repository.
Use React Native with Expo, TypeScript, SQLite, and HealthKit or Health Connect only when explicitly enabled; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: log user-chosen meals and activity, plan moderate routines, and show neutral summaries and trends without diagnosing, shaming, or enforcing restrictive goals.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create optional logs for activity, sleep, mood, energy, and personal notes with editable units.
Let the user build moderate routines and rest days without weight-loss targets, punishment, or competitive pressure.
Request health-platform permissions per data type and work fully without granting them.
Show weekly patterns and consistency with neutral language and no diagnostic or body-image judgments.
Add reminders that can be muted, data export, account-free local use, and full deletion.
Include a clear statement that the app is not medical care and should not replace qualified advice.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out medical diagnosis or treatment.
Deliberately leave out extreme exercise or restrictive-eating coaching.
Deliberately leave out wearable hardware, human coaching, and a large social network.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
